newsitem.title: USA: US Gulf Coast wallows in unsold West African crude.
newsitem.headline: US Gulf Coast wallows in unsold West African crude.

text.p: The U.S. Gulf Coast wallowed in unsold West African crude oil on Friday, giving buyers a sharp edge over sellers, traders said.
"I think there's plenty of crude out there, and people aren't being realistic about what they're asking," a Gulf Coast buyer said.

Among the cargoes looking for homes, a U.S. equity producer was offering a cargo each of Qua Iboe and Brass River for end-June arrival, asking around dated Brent plus $1.80 a barrel and dated Brent plus $2.00, respectively, traders said.
In addition, a European trading house was offering two Qua Iboe cargoes for July 1-5 delivery and one Bonny Light for July 10-15, asking around $1.85 a barrel over dated Brent, traders said.

Meanwhile, a distressed Saharan Blend cargo that a European trading house had been struggling to sell was heard to have been placed in storage, probably in the Caribbean. Unsuccessful bids were pegged around $1.25 under West Texas Intermediate/Cushing.

A rapidly narrowing transatlantic arbitrage all but cut off North Sea offerings into the Gulf Coast, although a lone company was still seen with July 8-12 barrels, asking WTI/Cushing minus 65-70 cents, traders said.
The July spread between WTI and Brent was a tight $1.05-15 a barrel Friday afternoon, down 25 cents from Thursday.
Even though dated Brent continued at a feeble 49 cents under the July quote on Friday, the arb was seen as unworkable.
In South America, Uruguay's state oil refiner ANCAP bought one million barrels of Mesa-30 crude from state Petroleos de Venezuela unit Lagoven, trade sources said.
ANCAP paid between $3.25 and $3.30 a barrel under WTI/Cushing for July 19-27 delivery.

ANCAP received some 30 offers from 13 different companies in this tender, three times the number of offers it usually receives. The turnout reinforced widely held perceptions that the market is oversupplied.
Many physical traders were riveted by the sharp drop in crude futures Friday afternoon. "Everybody's watching the screen today with the big drop," a trader said.
The July NYMEX price settled down 87 cents a barrel on Friday, after breaking through a second key support level to post a 15-month low for the front-month contract.
